h1:
Phichit Food Guide
The Shops Worth Stopping For
intro: Phichit is a town most people drive straight past, but if you actually pull over and eat, you'll find good stuff you won't get anywhere else — GI-listed Tha Khoi pomelo, old beef-ball noodle shops in town, fresh fish straight from the Nan River, and a four-flavour tamarind candy that's been around for over fifty years. We've pulled together what's worth eating in Phichit and where to go for it.

blocks.html: Phichit's food isn't flashy the way a big tourist town's is, but it has the charm of a small town where the good stuff clusters around the old centre and along the Nan River. Plenty of shops have been open for decades and are well known to locals. We've split things into categories — the famous fruit, the old noodle shops, freshwater river fish, and souvenirs to take home.

blocks.text: Tha Khoi Pomelo — The Town's GI Fruit

blocks.html: Say Phichit to a local and the first thing they think of is Tha Khoi pomelo. It's a heritage variety that's been registered as a GI (geographical indication) product. What sets it apart is the fine, firm flesh, a balanced sweet-tart flavour, plenty of juice, and few seeds — sometimes almost none. The main growing areas are around Pho Prathap Chang district and Tha Khoi sub-district, and the peak harvest runs from late in the year into early the next. Farm-gate prices swing with the season; in a good year you'll pay around ฿20 a kilo, and graded individual fruit in town runs a bit higher.

blocks.title: Tips for buying pomelo
blocks.html: For the best price and freshness, try going straight to the orchards around Pho Prathap Chang — some let you contact them and buy at the farm gate. Around Chinese New Year, people buy them in bulk for offerings, so prices climb and stock sells out fast. Go early in the season and you'll have an easier time picking.

blocks.title: Want to taste deeper? Try a Phichit food tour or cooking class
blocks.text: Half a day with a local who knows the lanes — or cooking a dish yourself — teaches you more than just eating. Book ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide.

blocks.html: In central Phichit there are several long-running noodle shops, especially around Charoen Si Road in the old part of town. Most make their own fishballs and meatballs and have been open long enough to have regulars going back generations.

items.name: Song Beef-Ball Noodles (Charoen Si Road)
items.blurb: An old shop in the Charoen Si Road community that makes its own balls in several styles — beef balls, stewed beef, and fresh beef. Order it as noodle soup or as a clear soup without noodles. The broth is simmered with beef until it's sweet and rounded, and it's still a regular stop for older Phichit folks.

items.name: Sanong Noodles (Pa Ho's shop)
items.blurb: Open since 1976 in the Charoen Si Road area, making its own balls. Known for the stewed beef and the clear-soup bowls — a legendary shop in the neighbourhood that the old-timers all know.

items.name: Pa Wun Pad Thai
items.blurb: A pad thai shop in town that's been going for over forty years. The standout is pad thai with duck egg — soft noodles with a balanced, old-school flavour, eaten with fresh bean sprouts and banana blossom.

blocks.html: The Nan River runs through Phichit, so freshwater fish dishes are another local highlight. Most fish restaurants sit along the main roads outside town, focusing on fresh fish cooked several ways — tom yum, fried with garlic, salt-grilled — at fair prices and generous portions, the way provincial restaurants tend to be.

items.name: Krua Pla Yai
items.blurb: A well-known spot on the Nakhon Sawan–Phitsanulok road (Thung Yai junction) with a wide range of river fish — tom yum with featherback fish, blanched clown featherback to dip, fried sheatfish with garlic, and grilled red tilapia. Generous portions and prices that don't sting.

items.name: Krua Te Te (River Fish)
items.blurb: Out around Thap Khlo on Highway 11, doing river fish well — redtail catfish and featherback. The dishes to order are the featherback fish cakes and the river-fish tom yum.

blocks.title: Ordering fish the smart way
blocks.html: River-fish restaurants usually price by the fish or by the kilo. If you're a group, order one fish split into two or three preparations — it works out cheaper and you get to try several flavours in one meal. Ask the weight before you order and it's easy to gauge the price.

items: Liang Hong Kee — traditional Chinese food out around Taphan Hin district, with oyster and fish dishes. Good for a family meal.
Krua Pa Lek (jungle food) — focused on jungle-style food and river fish, on the Nakhon Sawan–Phitsanulok road, with bold, homestyle flavours.
Phinthip rice and curry — an in-town shop with Thai curries, braised beef, and hotpot. Good for a quick lunch.

blocks.html: Before you leave, the Phichit souvenir people buy most is the four-flavour tamarind candy — a legendary sweet that's been made in town for over fifty years, sour-sweet-salty all in balance. You'll find it at souvenir shops across town, including the ones near the entrance to Bueng Si Fai.

items.name: Four-flavour tamarind candy
items.blurb: Phichit's most famous souvenir — sour, sweet, and salty in a single piece. It keeps well and makes a good gift, with prices starting in the tens of baht per box.

items.name: Tha Khoi pomelo / dried pomelo
items.blurb: Buy fresh pomelo whole, or the dried, processed version that keeps longer and is easier to carry home.

items: Sticky dried banana — processed cultivated banana, chewy and sticky, good for snacking.
Sweet ma-fai / Wang Sai Phun watermelon — seasonal local fruit you can find at markets in town.
Banana-leaf Thai sweets — in-town shops wrapping Thai desserts in banana leaf, good to grab for the road.

faq.q: What food should you try in Phichit?
faq.a: First up is the GI-listed Tha Khoi pomelo, with its firm flesh and sweet-tart flavour. After that, the old beef-ball noodle shops around Charoen Si Road, Nan River fish dishes, and souvenirs like the four-flavour tamarind candy.

faq.q: Where do you buy Tha Khoi pomelo and how much is it?
faq.a: The main growing areas are around Pho Prathap Chang district and Tha Khoi sub-district, where you can buy at the farm gate from late in the year into early the next. In a good year, farm-gate prices run around 20 THB a kilo; graded individual fruit in town costs a bit more.

faq.q: Where do you eat at the old noodle shops in Phichit town?
faq.a: The Charoen Si Road area is the hub for old noodle shops, including a beef-ball shop that makes its own and Sanong (Pa Ho's), open since 1976. Most are open from morning through lunch.

faq.q: Where should you go for freshwater fish in Phichit?
faq.a: The well-known river-fish restaurants tend to sit along the main roads — for example Krua Pla Yai on the Nakhon Sawan–Phitsanulok road and Krua Te Te around Thap Khlo. The featherback fish, soldier river barb, and grilled fish are all worth a try.

faq.q: What souvenirs should you buy in Phichit?
faq.a: The top pick is the four-flavour tamarind candy that's been made in town for over fifty years. After that, fresh Tha Khoi pomelo or its dried, processed version, and sticky dried banana. You'll find them at souvenir shops in town and around Bueng Si Fai.
